theme: Sin and guilt offerings, the cost of atonement
readingInstruction: Read Leviticus 4:1-5:19. Yesterday’s offerings were voluntary gifts of worship. Today’s are required, because they deal with sin. Notice who sins, how, and what each offering costs.
settingTheScene: The first three offerings in Leviticus were “sweet-smelling” ones, freely given in worship. Chapters 4 and 5 describe two offerings that are required when someone has sinned: the sin offering, or purification offering, and the guilt offering, or reparation offering. These deal with unintentional sin, wrongs done without the person realizing it at the time. They show that sin has consequences even when it is not deliberate, and they show that God provides a way for it to be cleansed.
observation: The sin offering applies to anyone who sins “unintentionally” (4:2, 13, 22, 27).
The offering differs by rank: a bull for the anointed priest and for the whole congregation, a male goat for a leader, and a female goat or lamb for a common person (4:3, 14, 22-23, 27-28).
For the priest and congregation, blood is sprinkled before the veil and put on the horns of the altar of incense (4:6-7, 17-18).
The person lays a hand on the head of the animal and kills it (4:4, 24, 29).
“And the priest shall make atonement for him, and he shall be forgiven” (4:20, 26, 31, 35).
The remains of the bull for the priest or congregation are burned outside the camp (4:11-12, 21).
For those who cannot afford an animal, there are provisions for birds and even fine flour (5:7-13).
The guilt offering requires restitution plus a fifth of the value, along with a ram (5:14-6:7).
interpretation:
The first thing to notice is how seriously Leviticus takes sin. Even unintentional sin requires a sacrifice. This is surprising to modern readers. We often think that sin matters only when it is deliberate. Leviticus says that sin has an objective weight, and that it defiles. This is part of what it means that God is holy: he is so pure that even accidental contact with sin makes a person unclean. The text is teaching us that sin is not just about our intentions.

The second thing is the scale of the offerings. The cost rises with the person’s position. A priest who sins brings a bull, just as the whole community does. Why? Because the sin of a leader affects everyone. The more influence a person has, the heavier the consequences of his sin. A common person brings a goat or lamb, and a poor person a bird. God’s grace is flexible, but his standard of holiness is not.

The third is the blood on the altar of incense and before the veil. The blood goes closer to God’s presence when the sin involves the priest or the whole people. It shows that sin does more than offend an individual. It pollutes the sanctuary itself. That is why the Day of Atonement, which you will read in a few days, includes cleansing the tabernacle.

The fourth is the repeated refrain: “and he shall be forgiven.” It is the goal of the chapters. Sacrifice is not just a way of paying a price. It is a way of being forgiven. The sinner lays his hand on the animal’s head, the animal dies in his place, the priest applies the blood, and the person is cleansed. The worshiper leaves forgiven.

The guilt offering adds a lesson. Sin against a neighbor requires more than a sacrifice. It requires restitution, repaying what was taken, with a fifth added. Forgiveness from God does not cancel the duty to make things right with people.
connection: Hebrews 13:11-12 says that the bodies of the animals for the sin offering were burned outside the camp, “so Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood.” Paul says that God “made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). The word for “sin offering” in the Greek Old Testament is the same as the word for “sin” there. Isaiah 53:10 says the servant’s life is made “an offering for guilt.” Zacchaeus’ restitution (Luke 19:8) shows the same principle.
application:
Reflect on whether you take unintentional sin seriously. Ask God to show you something you have not noticed.

Think of a wrong you have done to someone. Is there something you could do to make it right?

Thank God that the sin offering is finished in Christ, and that you can say “and he shall be forgiven” about yourself.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to forgive the sins you do not see.
Thank Jesus for being sacrificed outside the gate for you.
Ask him to show you what you need to make right.
